For your 5-person B2B team, I would not start on the highest tier of any CRM. Start with the lowest paid plan that covers email sync + follow-ups + useful pipeline reporting, then upgrade only when you hit a real limitation.

My recommendation
CRM	Start with	Why
Pipedrive	Growth	Best fit if sales + follow-up is the main job
HubSpot	Sales Hub Starter	Best if you want CRM + marketing/website ecosystem
Zoho CRM	Standard	Best value if you want lots of CRM functionality cheaply
🥇 Pipedrive Growth — my pick

For a 5-person sales team, I'd start with Growth, not Essential.

You want the email sync, sales automation and follow-up capabilities rather than buying a cheap plan and discovering that the workflows you actually need are locked behind an upgrade.

Your setup would be:

5 reps → 1 pipeline → Gmail/Outlook sync → automated follow-ups → manager dashboard

You don't need advanced customization initially.

🥈 HubSpot Sales Hub Starter

HubSpot is the better choice if your sales process is going to connect closely with website leads, forms, marketing, customer lifecycle and inbound leads.

Current HubSpot pricing lists Sales Hub Starter from $20/month per seat, although HubSpot's packaging and feature limits vary by product/seat, so check the exact checkout configuration. 
Legal Center

For five seats, that's roughly $100/month before taxes at the listed starting price.

🥉 Zoho CRM Standard

Zoho is surprisingly strong for the money. Its current India pricing shows ₹800/user/month for Standard when billed annually, including email integration, mass emails, multiple pipelines and sales forecasting. Professional is ₹1,400/user/month. 
Zoho

For five people:

Standard ≈ ₹4,000/month

That's excellent value if you're comfortable with a slightly more complex interface.

The hidden costs I'd check before signing

This is actually more important than the headline price.

1. Email automation limits

Ask:

"Does this exact plan include automated multi-step follow-up sequences?"

Not just email integration.

There's a big difference between:

CRM can send emails

and

CRM can automatically send:

Email 1 → wait 3 days → no reply → Email 2 → wait 5 days → Email 3 → create task for salesperson.

That's the functionality I'd make sure is included.

2. Number of users/seats

Check whether:

all 5 salespeople need paid seats

manager/admin seats cost the same

read-only/reporting users are free

automation users count as seats

Don't assume "5-person team" means exactly five paid licenses.

3. Email sending limits

There are usually separate considerations for:

1-to-1 sales emails

automated sequences

bulk/marketing emails

monthly email volume

If you're doing outbound prospecting, don't use a CRM's marketing email system as a substitute for a proper outbound email infrastructure.

4. Reporting limits

Check whether your plan lets you create:

pipeline by salesperson

pipeline by stage

monthly forecast

won/lost analysis

conversion rates

aging/stale deals

activity/follow-up reports

You don't need 100 reports. You need 5–8 useful ones.

5. Automation limits

Check the number of:

workflows

automation runs

sequences

active automations

actions per automation

This is where cheap plans can become frustrating.

6. WhatsApp / calling / third-party integrations

If your team eventually wants WhatsApp, phone calling, LinkedIn, Google Workspace, Slack, etc., check whether those are native or require a paid integration/third-party tool.

Zoho, for example, advertises 1,200+ integrations, which is a genuine advantage if you expect a more connected sales stack. 
Zoho

7. Annual vs monthly pricing

Don't compare:

$14/month

against

$20/month

until you know whether one number assumes annual billing.

I'd calculate the actual 12-month cash cost for five users, including taxes.

What I'd do in your position

I'd run a 14-day side-by-side test with the same 20–30 leads:

Pipedrive Growth vs HubSpot Sales Hub Starter vs Zoho Standard

Give each salesperson the same workflow:

Import 30 leads

Assign owner

Send first email

Schedule follow-up

Move deal through pipeline

Mark lost/won

Manager checks dashboard

Then ask the team one question:

"Which one would you actually keep updated every day?"

For a 5-person team coming from spreadsheets, adoption is more important than having 200 CRM features.

My final ranking: Pipedrive Growth → HubSpot Starter → Zoho Standard.

And if keeping the monthly bill very low matters, Zoho Standard is the value winner at roughly ₹4,000/month for five users based on its current India annual pricing. 
Zoho

If your priority is hands-on SQL + spreadsheet work, I’d rank them:

1. DataCamp → best for practice
2. Udemy → best value for project-based learning
3. Coursera → best structured career path/certificate

	Coursera	Udemy	DataCamp
SQL practice	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Spreadsheet/Excel	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐
Real projects	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Beginner friendly	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Structured curriculum	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Learning by doing	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Certificate value	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐
Best for working professionals	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
1. DataCamp — my pick for SQL

DataCamp is particularly strong if you want to actually write SQL rather than watch someone explain SQL.

Its current Associate Data Analyst in SQL track is about 39 hours, starts from zero, and progresses through filtering, aggregation, joins, subqueries and window functions. It includes hands-on projects using realistic datasets. 
DataCamp
+1

It also has dedicated projects where you work through datasets and build analyses from start to finish. 
DataCamp Support
+1

Best for:
Learn → immediately practice → repeat

Weakness: Excel/spreadsheets aren't its biggest strength.

2. Udemy — best for Excel + practical projects

Udemy is probably the best choice if you want one relatively inexpensive course that teaches Excel + SQL + dashboards through projects.

For example, the current Data Analysis | SQL, Tableau, Power BI & Excel | Real Projects course has 41K+ students, a 4.6 rating, and covers SQL, Excel, Power BI, Tableau and real-world projects. 
Udemy

There's also a newer Excel + SQL + Python bootcamp that explicitly follows:

Excel → SQL → Python → real projects, with Excel formulas, pivot tables, dashboards, SQL joins and practical datasets. 
Udemy

Best for:
I want to build things and follow along with an instructor

Weakness: Udemy quality varies enormously between instructors, so you need to choose carefully.

3. Coursera — best overall foundation

The Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate is more structured than either Udemy or DataCamp. It covers spreadsheets, SQL, data cleaning, visualization and broader analyst workflows, with a case study you can use as a portfolio piece. 
Coursera
+1

Google says the program is designed for beginners and can be completed in roughly 3–6 months, with under 10 hours/week. In India, Google currently lists the subscription at $20/month after a 7-day trial. 
Grow with Google

Best for:
I'm starting completely from scratch and want someone to tell me what to learn in what order

Weakness: It's broader and slower. If your only goal is becoming good at SQL quickly, DataCamp is more efficient.

What I'd do in your situation

If you're a working professional starting from zero, I wouldn't spend 6 months passively completing a certificate.

I'd use:

Month 1 — Excel/Google Sheets

XLOOKUP

SUMIFS/COUNTIFS

IF/IFS

Pivot tables

Data cleaning

Charts

Basic dashboards

Month 2 — SQL

SELECT / WHERE

GROUP BY

CASE WHEN

JOINs

CTEs

Subqueries

Window functions

Month 3 — Projects
Build 3 projects:

Sales analysis

Customer/user cohort analysis

Marketing or product analytics

My actual recommendation

If you want one platform: DataCamp

If you want the cheapest practical route: Udemy + your own projects

If you want a recognised certificate + structured beginner curriculum: Coursera / Google Data Analytics

For SQL specifically, I'd choose DataCamp. For Excel specifically, I'd choose Udemy. For overall data-analytics career preparation, I'd choose Coursera.

And I wouldn't learn Python initially. Excel/Sheets → SQL → dashboards → Python is a much easier progression for someone starting from scratch.
